newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH KGHM DROPS PLANS OF CAPITAL INCREASE - CEO.
newsitem.headline: POLISH KGHM DROPS PLANS OF CAPITAL INCREASE - CEO.

text.p: Poland's KGHM copper concern, to be floated domestically and internationally in mid-year, has for now abandoned plans of a new share issue which would raise its capital, KGHM's president said.

"After analysing the firm's financial needs we abandoned plans of a B series issue which would raise KGHM's capital. But I cannot exclude doing it in the future," Stanislaw Siewierski told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily.

In October last year KGHM's board proposed to issue new shares alongside with or soon after the sale of existing stock to boost the company's capital because all the money from the flotation would go the treasury's coffers.
Siewierski also said he did not consider KGHM's drop in net profit in 1996 as bad considering the fall in world copper prices from 1995 record levels.
KGHM's net in 1996 tumbled to 147.2 million zlotys from 481.9 million in 1995. Siewierski also said the much worse results were due to provisions the company made towards potential future expenses.

"We decided that because of preparations for privatisation we have to make provisions...so that in the future investors would not have to pay, for example, a delayed fine for environment pollution from current profits," Siewierski said.
KGHM alloted 274 million zlotys to provisions in 1996 against 5.7 million in 1995.
Siewierski reiterated the treasury ministry's statements that the privatisaiotn of the company was on track and that it should make its bourse debut in June.

"I expect the government will make the final decisions in April...The issue prospectus should be ready by the end of the month...and then everything is in the hands of the Securities Commission," he said.

Siewierski said the final division of tranches for domestic and international flotation would be determined by the council of ministers, but that he would like to see 51 percent of KGHM's stock in private hands.
"Employees will get 15 percent for free and at least 36 percent can be sold on bourses in Poland and abroad," he said.

Siewierski said he hoped the pending reform of the pensions system would pave the way for placing shares of employees in pension funds and therefore solve the potential problem of mass sales of shares by workers after a two-year moratorium.
"However, if work in parliament (on the reform) is delayed, we will present our own project of a KGHM pension fund, which is ready," Siewierski said.
